cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: Latin word order is much freer than English because grammatical relationships are shown by case endings, not position. The most common order is Subject-Object-Verb (SOV).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: The verb typically comes at or near the end of a Latin sentence, which is the biggest difference from English SVO order.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: Adjectives must agree with the noun they modify in gender, number, and case (GNC): puella bona (good girl, fem. nom. sg.), servum bonum (good slave, masc. acc. sg.).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: Relative clauses use the relative pronoun qui, quae, quod (who, which, that) which must agree with its antecedent in gender and number, but takes its case from its own clause.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: Common conjunctions: et (and), sed (but), aut (or), -que (and, attached to the second word), tamen (however), igitur (therefore), nam/quia (because).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: Indirect statement (accusative + infinitive construction): the subject of the reported speech is in the accusative, and the verb is an infinitive (e.g. dicit puellam venire — he says the girl is coming).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: Purpose clauses use ut + subjunctive for positive purpose (in order to) and ne + subjunctive for negative purpose (in order not to).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: Result clauses use ut + subjunctive with a word like tam, tantus, or ita in the main clause (so...that...).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: Temporal clauses use cum + subjunctive (when/since/although, depending on context) and postquam/ubi + indicative (after/when).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentence Structure & Translation
cards.back: When translating, read the whole sentence first, identify the verb, then work out the case of each noun to determine its function.

cards.front: What should you know about gcse latin exam tips — sentence structure & translation?
cards.back: 1. For Sentence Structure & Translation, use a range of vocabulary and complex grammatical structures to access higher marks 2. Check verb tenses, agreements and word order carefully in your written work 3. In translation tasks, translate meaning rather than word-for-word 4. When writing about Sentence Structure & Translation, include opinions and justifications, not just descriptions 5. For listening and reading, focus on key words and cognates to extract meaning
